title: Rabbi Akiva and Rachel
text:
Akiva was an unlearned shepherd working for Kalba Savua, one of the richest men in Jerusalem. Kalba Savua's daughter saw that he was modest and good, and asked him: if she betrothed herself to him, would he go and study Torah? He said yes. They married secretly. When her father found out, he threw her out of the house and vowed that she would get nothing from his property.

The Talmud says they were so poor in the winter that they slept on straw, and Akiva would pick the straw from her hair. He told her that if he could, he would give her a "Jerusalem of gold," a golden crown engraved with the city.

She sent him off to study. After twelve years he came home with twelve thousand students. As he approached, he overheard an old man mocking her for living as a widow while her husband was away. She answered that if he listened to her, he would study twelve more years. Hearing this, Akiva turned around and went back.

He returned after another twelve years with twenty four thousand students. She went out to meet him, in shabby clothes, and fell at his feet. His students tried to push her away, but Akiva stopped them: "What is mine and what is yours is hers." Kalba Savua, hearing of the great scholar, came to have his vow annulled and gave them half his wealth.
lesson: One partner's belief and sacrifice can make the other's achievement possible. When success comes, honor the person who made it possible.
people: Rabbi Akiva, his wife (traditionally called Rachel), Kalba Savua
caveat: The Talmudic accounts are legendary and differ in details, and the name Rachel comes from later tradition.
